pregunta: Where can we land and live on the Moon, and is there water for astronauts?

objetivos.necesitas: A high-resolution camera and an instrument that measures elevation (laser).

objetivos.nombre: Search for water ice at the poles
objetivos.necesitas: Sensors that detect hydrogen, extreme cold, or ice: neutron, temperature, ultraviolet, radar.

crucero_texto: The trip to the Moon takes about 4 days. We'll alert you when something requires your decision.
llegada_texto: We've arrived at the Moon. We must brake so its gravity captures us into orbit.

pistas.cohete: The Moon is close: a medium rocket is enough. Pick the cheapest one that can lift your spacecraft.
pistas.propulsion: You need 1,300 m/s of delta-v to reach the Moon and brake. Check the bar: do you really need the biggest tank?
pistas.energia: Near Earth there is plenty of sunlight: small solar panels are enough and cost less.
pistas.antena: The LROC camera generates tons of data. Can your antenna keep up with downlinking it?
pistas.blindaje: Radiation near the Moon is low. Is it worth paying for shielding?
pistas.instrumentos: Check the tags on each instrument: they show which objective they support.

cohete.texto: It launches your spacecraft off Earth. Each rocket has a maximum payload capacity: if your spacecraft is too heavy, it won't launch. More powerful rockets cost more money.

propulsion.texto: Δv (delta-v) is how much the spacecraft can change its velocity using its own engine, in meters per second. Reaching the Moon and braking into orbit requires a specific amount. More propellant gives more delta-v... but also adds mass.

energia.texto: Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity for the flight computer, heaters, and payload instruments. Near Earth there is plenty of sunlight; far from the Sun, like at Jupiter, very little light arrives.

antena.texto: All science data must be downlinked to Earth via radio to ground stations. A larger antenna transmits more data per day. If your instruments generate more data than you can downlink, that science is lost.

blindaje.texto: High-energy particles travel through space and damage electronics. Near the Moon there is little; near Jupiter, a huge amount. Shielding protects the payload, but adds mass.

instrumentos.texto: They are the eyes of the mission. Each instrument supports one or more objectives (check their tags). They add mass, cost money, and consume power: choose the ones that answer the mission question.

crucero.texto: Events will happen during the flight: take your time and decide carefully. The power console shows whether you have surplus electricity or a deficit; if the battery runs out, the spacecraft enters safe mode.

llegada.texto: To enter lunar orbit, you must perform a braking burn with your engine right as you arrive. If you brake too little, you fly past; if you brake too much, you end up in an orbit that is too low.

operacion.texto: Each orbit around the Moon gathers data. You decide when to end the mission and how to do it.

por_que.energia: Near Earth there is abundant sunlight: LRO used a single solar panel, much smaller than Juno's massive wings.
por_que.antena: LRO generates so much data (especially photos) that it needs a high-speed, high-gain antenna for downlink.
por_que.blindaje: Radiation near the Moon is low: there is no need for a heavy radiation vault like Juno's.
por_que.propulsion: The Moon is close: it needed much less propellant than a mission to Jupiter.
por_que.cohete: An Atlas V 401 with no solid boosters: enough for the Moon. It shared the ride with another mission (LCROSS).
por_que.orbita: LRO mapped the Moon from a circular polar orbit at 50 km altitude and later moved to an elliptical orbit to save propellant.
por_que.final: LRO is still operating more than 15 years later and is crucial for choosing landing sites for Artemis astronauts.

briefing: Welcome to Mission Control! This is your training mission.
Mission question: where can we land and live on the Moon, and is there water for astronauts?
You will investigate the SURFACE and WATER ICE at the poles: pay close attention to cameras and ice sensors.
You have $650 million. I'll explain each concept the first time it appears.

eventos.texto: The spacecraft separated from the rocket and is tumbling out of control: the battery is draining. Deploy the panel now?

opciones.resultado: Successful deployment. The panel begins charging the battery.
Safer, but the battery drained significantly while waiting.

eventos.texto: We're slightly off course. A short engine burn will put us back on track to the Moon. How much thrust do we apply?
eventos.resultado_ok: Course corrected: heading straight for the Moon.
eventos.resultado_mal: We'll have to correct again: burned extra propellant.

eventos.texto: An attitude sensor that tracks where the spacecraft is pointing failed, and the spacecraft entered safe mode. Reboot systems from the cockpit.

exito.resultado: Systems recovered. The spacecraft knows its orientation again.

fallo.resultado: Recovery took hours and we lost mission time.

eventos.texto: Now in lunar orbit. Flying lower reveals sharper details, but maintaining a low orbit burns propellant.

opciones.texto: Stay in low orbit indefinitely (more photos, risk of running out of propellant)
opciones.resultado_ok: It worked! More low-altitude passes and extra science collected.
opciones.resultado_mal: Propellant ran out sooner than expected: safe mode and vehicle damage.

opciones.texto: Map in low orbit, then transition to an elliptical orbit to save propellant
opciones.resultado: More total passes using less propellant. That's what the real LRO did.

final_texto: You finished the primary mission. The real LRO is still in orbit more than 15 years later and helps choose where astronauts will land.

orbitas.descripcion: A nearly circular orbit over both poles, very close to the surface.
orbitas.por_que: This was LRO's science orbit from 2009 to 2011: it gives the sharpest images, but mascons (patches of uneven gravity) pull it off course, so it needs frequent corrections, burns more fuel and lasts less.

orbitas.descripcion: A stretched orbit over the poles: it dips to 30 km above the south pole and climbs to 180 km above the north pole.
orbitas.por_que: LRO has flown this orbit since December 2011 to save fuel. It lasts many years, although the coverage is a bit less even.

orbitas.descripcion: A high circular orbit over the poles, far from the mascons.
orbitas.por_que: It is stable and needs almost no corrections, so it saves fuel and lasts longer. In exchange, you see less detail from that far away and the science goes down.
